title: Tokyo Travel Guide for First-Timers
excerpt: Everything a first-time visitor needs to know about Tokyo — where to go, how to get around, where to stay, and how long to spend.
content:
Tokyo is one of the world's great cities — vast, fast, endlessly varied, and far easier to navigate than its size suggests. For a first-time visitor it can feel overwhelming, so here's the orientation that ties it all together: what Tokyo is, how to move around, and how to spend your days.

Getting your bearings

Tokyo is a collection of distinct districts strung along and inside the JR Yamanote loop line, the circular train route that connects most of the areas you'll want to visit. Learn the loop and the city clicks into place: Shinjuku and Shibuya on the west side, Tokyo Station and Ginza to the east-center, Asakusa and the old town to the northeast. Get a Suica or Pasmo IC card on arrival and the trains become effortless.

What to see

The essentials for a first trip: Senso-ji, the historic temple in Asakusa; the famous Shibuya Crossing; the immersive teamLab digital art museum; the serene Meiji Shrine beside Harajuku; and the view from Tokyo Skytree. Around these, each neighborhood has its own character worth wandering — youthful Harajuku, electric Akihabara, upscale Ginza.

Where to stay

Base yourself near the Yamanote loop. Shinjuku is the do-everything all-rounder, Shibuya is youthful and central, and Asakusa offers traditional charm and better value. Any of these keeps the whole city within easy reach.

How long to spend

Give Tokyo at least two to three days on a first trip — enough for the headline sights, a neighborhood or two to explore, and ideally a day trip to somewhere like Hakone or Nikko. You could easily spend a week and not run out of things to do, but two or three days covers the essentials before moving on to Kyoto.

Eating in Tokyo

Tokyo is one of the planet's best food cities, from Michelin-starred counters to humble ramen shops and izakaya pubs. Don't miss trying ramen, sushi, and the small plates of an izakaya. Remember there's no tipping, and it's polite not to eat while walking.

Practical tips

  • Trains stop running around midnight — plan your nights or budget for a taxi.
  • Carry some cash; not everywhere takes cards.
  • Stay quiet on trains and queue where marked.
  • Mapping apps work well for train routing in the city.

Plan your days

Group sights by area to save time, mix one big-ticket sight with neighborhood wandering each day, and book timed-entry experiences like teamLab ahead. With a little structure, Tokyo goes from overwhelming to exhilarating — the perfect start to a first trip to Japan.

title: 3 Days in Tokyo: The Perfect Itinerary
excerpt: A day-by-day 3-day Tokyo itinerary for first-timers, balancing the iconic sights, neighborhoods, and a day trip — without rushing.
content:
Three days is the sweet spot for a first taste of Tokyo — enough to hit the icons, soak up a couple of neighborhoods, and still have room to breathe. Here's a balanced day-by-day plan you can follow or adapt.

Day 1: West side — Shibuya, Harajuku, Shinjuku

Start in Shibuya and walk the famous Shibuya Crossing, then head to nearby Harajuku for youth fashion and the peaceful Meiji Shrine in its forest setting. In the afternoon move to Shinjuku — explore the shops and, in the evening, the atmospheric lantern-lit alleys of Omoide Yokocho for dinner. A great high-energy introduction to modern Tokyo.

Day 2: Old Tokyo — Asakusa, Skytree, Akihabara

Begin early at Senso-ji in Asakusa, approaching through the Nakamise shopping street. Head to nearby Tokyo Skytree for the view, then over to Akihabara for the electronics-and-anime spectacle. If time allows, the Tsukiji Outer Market is great for a seafood lunch. This day balances tradition and quirk.

Day 3: Choose your adventure

For your third day, pick based on your interests:

  • teamLab + Ginza: the immersive digital art museum (book ahead), followed by upscale shopping and dining in Ginza.
  • Day trip: escape to Hakone for hot springs and Mt Fuji views, or Nikko for forest shrines, or Kamakura for the Great Buddha by the sea.

A day trip is highly recommended if the weather's good — it adds variety and a taste of Japan beyond the capital.

Tips to make it flow

  • Get a Suica/Pasmo IC card on day one and use the Yamanote loop to move between areas.
  • Start mornings early at popular sights (Senso-ji, Meiji Shrine) to beat crowds.
  • Group each day by geography to minimize backtracking.
  • Book teamLab and any tours in advance.

Adapting the plan

If you have a fourth day, add the day trip and the teamLab/Ginza day rather than choosing. If you're tighter on time, day three can be trimmed. However you shape it, three days gives you a satisfying first taste of Tokyo before the bullet train carries you on to Kyoto.

title: Tokyo with Kids: A Family Travel Guide
excerpt: Tokyo is a fantastic family destination. Here are the most kid-friendly sights, practical tips, and how to keep everyone happy.
content:
Tokyo is a surprisingly great city for families — clean, safe, endlessly novel, and full of attractions that delight kids and adults alike. With a little planning, traveling here with children is smooth and genuinely fun. Here's how to approach it.

Why Tokyo works for families

Japan's exceptional safety, spotless public spaces, reliable trains, and abundance of conveniences make it easy to travel with kids. Children are generally welcomed, convenience stores are everywhere for quick snacks and supplies, and the sheer novelty of the city keeps young travelers engaged.

Kid-friendly sights and experiences

  • teamLab — the immersive, interactive digital art is mesmerizing for all ages (book timed tickets ahead).
  • Tokyo Skytree — the sky-high view is a hit, with shopping and an aquarium at its base.
  • Theme parks — Tokyo's famous theme parks just outside the city are a major draw for families (plan a full day each).
  • Ueno — a large park with a zoo and museums, good for a relaxed day.
  • Akihabara — a wonderland for kids into games, anime, and gadgets.
  • Animal cafes and character shops — plenty of novelty experiences kids love.

Practical tips for families

  • Trains: kids often love them, and strollers are manageable, though some stations have lots of stairs — look for elevators, and consider a baby carrier for busy times.
  • Food: Japan is easy for picky eaters — plain rice, noodles, convenience-store snacks, and familiar chains are everywhere. Highchairs and kids' options exist at family restaurants.
  • Supplies: diapers, wipes, and baby food are easy to buy; pharmacies and convenience stores are plentiful.
  • Rest: the city is intense, so build in downtime — parks, your hotel, or a relaxed afternoon.

Getting around with children

The train system is the easiest way to move, and an IC card works for kids too (children's fares apply). Avoid rush hours with little ones when you can, as trains get very crowded. Taxis are clean and safe for tired-kid moments but pricier.

Pacing the trip

The biggest tip with kids is not to overpack the schedule. One or two main activities a day, plenty of snack and rest breaks, and flexibility for naps or meltdowns will keep everyone happier than trying to see everything. Tokyo rewards a relaxed pace — and there's always a convenience store or park around the corner when you need a reset.

title: Tokyo Nightlife: The Best Evening Districts
excerpt: From neon-lit alleys to skyline bars, here's where to spend an evening out in Tokyo — and what each district is known for.
content:
Tokyo after dark is a spectacle of its own — neon, tiny bars, izakaya, and skyline views. Whether you want a quiet drink, a lively night out, or just atmospheric wandering, here are the districts to know.

Shinjuku

Shinjuku is the heart of Tokyo nightlife. The famous Golden Gai is a warren of tiny, characterful bars packed into narrow lanes, while Omoide Yokocho ('Memory Lane') offers atmospheric alley dining and drinks under red lanterns. The wider Kabukicho area is the city's biggest entertainment district — vibrant and intense, though worth normal caution late at night. Great for bar-hopping and soaking up the neon.

Shibuya

Shibuya is younger and trend-driven, with countless bars, clubs, and izakaya around the famous crossing. It's lively and accessible, popular with a youthful crowd, and an easy place to start an evening. The area stays busy late and connects well to the rest of the city.

Roppongi

Roppongi is known as the most international nightlife district, with clubs and bars popular among visitors. It's lively and English-friendly, though like any major nightlife zone it's worth being sensible about overly pushy touts and inflated bar tabs — stick to reputable venues.

Ginza

For a more refined evening, Ginza offers upscale bars, including elegant cocktail lounges and hotel sky bars with city views. It's polished, quieter, and ideal for a sophisticated night out rather than a raucous one.

Izakaya: the local way

Wherever you are, the quintessential Tokyo evening is at an izakaya — a Japanese pub serving small plates alongside beer, sake, and highballs. They range from cheap chains to refined specialists, and they're the most authentic way to eat and drink like a local. Just settle in, order a few dishes at a time, and enjoy.

Practical night-out tips

  • Trains stop around midnight; plan your route home or budget for a taxi.
  • Carry cash — many small bars don't take cards.
  • Some bars charge a small seating/cover fee (otoshi); this is normal.
  • Be cautious of touts steering you to specific bars in nightlife zones.
  • There's no tipping.

Choosing your night

For neon and tiny bars, head to Shinjuku. For a youthful buzz, Shibuya. For international clubs, Roppongi. For refined cocktails, Ginza. Or simply find a good izakaya wherever you are — that's Tokyo nightlife at its most genuine.

title: Kyoto Travel Guide for First-Timers
excerpt: Everything a first-time visitor needs to know about Kyoto — its temples, neighborhoods, how to get around, and how long to stay.
content:
Kyoto is Japan's cultural heart — a city of temples, shrines, gardens, and preserved old streets that served as the imperial capital for over a thousand years. It rewards a slower pace than Tokyo. Here's the orientation a first-time visitor needs.

Getting your bearings

Unlike Tokyo, Kyoto has no single train loop. The sights are spread out — the eastern hills (Higashiyama, Gion) on one side, Arashiyama to the west, Fushimi Inari to the south, Kinkaku-ji to the northwest. You'll get around by a mix of buses, the subway, and walking, all covered by your Suica or Pasmo IC card. The smart strategy is to group sights by area and tackle one zone per day.

What to see

The essentials: Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion; Fushimi Inari with its thousands of red torii gates; Kiyomizu-dera and the atmospheric Higashiyama streets leading up to it; the Arashiyama bamboo grove; and an evening wander through Gion, the historic geisha district. These define a first visit.

Where to stay

For atmosphere, stay in Gion or Higashiyama, within walking distance of major temples. For transport convenience and day trips, the Kyoto Station area is ideal. Downtown is a lively central middle-ground, and Arashiyama trades convenience for scenery and calm.

How long to spend

Give Kyoto at least two to three days — enough for the major temples grouped by area, an evening in Gion, and ideally a day trip to Nara, Osaka, or Himeji. Kyoto rewards lingering, so don't rush it into a single day.

Eating in Kyoto

Kyoto has a refined food culture: kaiseki multi-course dining, matcha sweets, simmered tofu (yudofu), and the food stalls of Nishiki Market. Pontocho Alley is a magical riverside lane for dinner. As everywhere in Japan, there's no tipping.

Practical tips

  • Wear comfortable shoes — you'll walk a lot between and within sights.
  • Start early at popular temples (Fushimi Inari, Kinkaku-ji) to beat crowds.
  • Buses can be slow in peak times; the subway and trains are faster where they go.
  • Be respectful in Gion — don't chase or block geiko/maiko.

Plan your days

Group temples by district, start early, and balance temple-heavy mornings with relaxed afternoons in old streets or markets. Done right, Kyoto is the soulful counterpoint to Tokyo and often travelers' favorite part of a first trip to Japan.

title: 2 Days in Kyoto: The Perfect Itinerary
excerpt: A focused 2-day Kyoto itinerary for first-timers — the essential temples, the bamboo grove, and an evening in Gion, grouped to save time.
content:
Two days in Kyoto is enough to experience its essentials if you plan smartly — the key is grouping sights by area so you're not crisscrossing the city. Here's a focused day-by-day plan for first-timers.

Day 1: Eastern Kyoto (Higashiyama and Gion)

Spend your first day on the atmospheric eastern side. Start early at Fushimi Inari, walking up through its tunnels of red torii gates before the crowds build. Then head to the Higashiyama district and wander the preserved sloping lanes — Ninenzaka and Sannenzaka — up to Kiyomizu-dera, the grand hillside temple with sweeping views. In the late afternoon and evening, explore Gion, the historic geisha district, and have dinner along the riverside Pontocho Alley. This day captures old Kyoto at its most beautiful.

Day 2: West and north (Arashiyama and Kinkaku-ji)

Begin in Arashiyama on the western edge — walk the famous bamboo grove early, then enjoy the riverside scenery and temples (and the monkey park if you like). In the afternoon, cross the city to Kinkaku-ji, the dazzling Golden Pavilion reflected in its pond. If you have energy left, nearby Ryoan-ji's famous rock garden makes a serene addition. This day pairs Kyoto's natural beauty with its most iconic temple.

Making two days work

  • Get a Suica/Pasmo IC card for buses, subway, and trains.
  • Start each day early — popular sights are far more pleasant and photogenic before mid-morning.
  • Group by area (east one day, west/north the next) to minimize travel time.
  • Wear comfortable walking shoes.

If you have a third day

Add a day trip to Nara for the giant Buddha and friendly deer, or to Osaka for food and energy, or Himeji for Japan's finest castle. A third day also lets you slow down and add sights like Nijo Castle or the Philosopher's Path. But even in two well-planned days, you'll come away having seen the best of Kyoto.

title: Kyoto Temples: Which Ones to Prioritize
excerpt: Kyoto has hundreds of temples and shrines. Here's how to choose the ones worth your limited time on a first visit.
content:
Kyoto has hundreds of temples and shrines — far more than anyone can see in a single trip. The key to enjoying them rather than burning out is choosing a handful of standouts and grouping them by area. Here's how to prioritize for a first visit.

The must-see shortlist

Fushimi Inari Taisha

The shrine of thousands of vermilion torii gates winding up a mountainside. Iconic, free to enter, and unlike anything else. Go early or late to avoid the densest crowds. Top priority.

Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion)

The gold-leaf-covered temple mirrored in its pond — Kyoto's most famous image. The visit is short, making it easy to combine with other northwest sights. A first-trip essential.

Kiyomizu-dera

A grand wooden temple on a hillside with a famous viewing veranda, beautiful in every season and reached via the lovely Higashiyama streets. The walk up is half the pleasure.

Strong additions if you have time

  • Ginkaku-ji (Silver Pavilion): an elegant temple with refined gardens, at the end of the scenic Philosopher's Path.
  • Ryoan-ji: home to Japan's most famous Zen rock garden — contemplative and minimalist.
  • Tenryu-ji: a major Zen temple in Arashiyama with a celebrated garden, right by the bamboo grove.
  • Nanzen-ji: a large, peaceful temple complex with a striking brick aqueduct.

How to avoid temple fatigue

Seeing too many temples in a row blurs them together. A few strategies help: group by area (Fushimi Inari and Kiyomizu/Higashiyama in the east; Kinkaku-ji and Ryoan-ji in the northwest; Tenryu-ji in Arashiyama), mix in non-temple experiences like markets, gardens, and old streets, and limit yourself to two or three major temples a day. Quality over quantity makes the visits memorable.

Practical notes

  • Many temples charge a small entrance fee; carry coins and small bills.
  • Opening hours are often limited (many close by late afternoon) — plan accordingly.
  • Dress respectfully and follow posted etiquette, especially in active places of worship.
  • Start early for the most famous sites to enjoy them with fewer crowds.

The bottom line

For a first visit, prioritize Fushimi Inari, Kinkaku-ji, and Kiyomizu-dera, then add one or two more based on your route and interest. Group them geographically, pace yourself, and Kyoto's temples will be a highlight rather than a blur.

title: Shinjuku Area Guide: What to Do in Tokyo's Busiest Hub
excerpt: Shinjuku packs nightlife, shopping, parks, and the world's busiest station into one district. Here's how to make sense of it.
content:
Shinjuku is Tokyo at its most concentrated — a district that crams together neon nightlife, vast shopping, skyscrapers, and a beautiful park, all around one of the world's busiest train stations. It can be dizzying, so here's how to navigate it and what not to miss.

The station (don't panic)

Shinjuku Station is enormous and famously confusing, with dozens of exits. The trick: know which exit you need before you arrive (follow signs to landmarks or compass directions), and don't be afraid to surface and reorient. Once outside, the district is walkable.

What to do

  • Shinjuku Gyoen: one of Tokyo's loveliest parks, a serene escape with gardens — gorgeous in cherry blossom season.
  • Omoide Yokocho: atmospheric lantern-lit alleys of tiny eateries and bars, perfect for an evening.
  • Golden Gai: a warren of minuscule themed bars, a Tokyo nightlife institution.
  • Kabukicho: the big, brash entertainment district — vibrant and intense at night.
  • Skyscraper district & observation decks: including free city views from some government building observatories.
  • Shopping: huge department stores, electronics megastores, and endless retail.

Where it fits in your trip

Shinjuku is a top choice to stay thanks to its transport links and all-in-one convenience, and a top choice to go out at night. By day it's strong for shopping and the park; by night it's the heart of Tokyo nightlife. Many travelers pass through its station constantly regardless of where they stay.

Practical tips

  • Use station lockers or your hotel to avoid hauling shopping around.
  • Trains stop around midnight — plan your night accordingly.
  • In Kabukicho at night, ignore touts and stick to reputable venues.
  • The west side is skyscrapers and calm; the east side is shopping and nightlife.

Bottom line

Shinjuku rewards a bit of fearlessness — embrace the energy, pick a couple of targets (the park by day, the alleys by night), and don't let the giant station intimidate you. It's Tokyo's beating heart and an essential part of the city.

title: Shibuya & Harajuku Area Guide
excerpt: Youthful, fashionable, and endlessly walkable — here's what to do in Tokyo's Shibuya and Harajuku districts, from the famous crossing to Meiji Shrine.
content:
Shibuya and Harajuku sit side by side on Tokyo's west side and together form the city's youthful, fashion-forward heart. They're easy to combine into a single day of wandering. Here's what to see in each.

Shibuya

Shibuya is anchored by the world-famous Shibuya Crossing, the scramble intersection where crowds surge across in every direction. Walk it once, then watch the spectacle from a surrounding cafe or viewpoint. Nearby is the Hachiko statue, a beloved meeting spot, and endless shopping, dining, and nightlife. Shibuya is energetic, trend-driven, and a great base or night-out destination.

What to do in Shibuya

  • Experience the crossing from street level and from above.
  • Shop the department stores and youth-fashion buildings.
  • Explore the side streets for cafes, restaurants, and bars.
  • Take in a city view from one of the newer observation decks.

Harajuku

A short walk or one train stop from Shibuya, Harajuku is the center of Tokyo's youth and street fashion. Takeshita Street is its famously colorful, crowded pedestrian lane packed with quirky shops, crepes, and trends. Just beyond, Omotesando offers a more upscale, tree-lined boulevard of designer boutiques and architecture.

Meiji Shrine

The contrast that makes this area special: right beside busy Harajuku lies Meiji Shrine, set in a tranquil forest. The wooded approach and grand torii gates create one of the most peaceful spots in central Tokyo — a perfect counterpoint to the surrounding bustle. Don't skip it.

How to combine them

A natural plan: start with the calm of Meiji Shrine in the morning, wander Harajuku (Takeshita Street and Omotesando), then end in Shibuya for the crossing and an evening out. It's an easy, walkable progression from serene to electric, and showcases Tokyo's range in a single day.

Practical tips

  • Weekends are extremely crowded in Harajuku — go early or on a weekday if you can.
  • It's all walkable, but the JR Yamanote line connects the stations if you tire.
  • Great area for people-watching and street food (just don't eat while walking).

title: Asakusa & Old Tokyo Area Guide
excerpt: Asakusa is Tokyo's most traditional district, home to Senso-ji temple and old-town charm. Here's what to see and do.
content:
Asakusa is where Tokyo holds onto its past — a district of temples, traditional shops, and old-town atmosphere on the city's northeast side. It's the best place to feel historic Tokyo, and a favorite base for travelers who prefer charm and value over glitz. Here's what to do.

Senso-ji

The centerpiece is Senso-ji, Tokyo's oldest and most famous temple. You enter through the iconic Kaminarimon ('Thunder Gate') with its giant red lantern, then walk the Nakamise shopping street — lined with stalls selling traditional snacks and souvenirs — up to the grand temple hall. Go early in the morning to experience it before the crowds. It's the heart of Asakusa and a Tokyo essential.

Around the temple

  • Nakamise Street: great for street snacks (try freshly made sweets) and traditional souvenirs.
  • Backstreets: wander beyond the main drag for craft shops, old-style eateries, and a quieter feel.
  • Sumida River: nearby for riverside walks and boat cruises.
  • Rickshaw rides: a fun, if touristy, way to tour the old streets.
  • Kimono rental: popular here for strolling the traditional setting in style.

Tokyo Skytree nearby

Just across the river from Asakusa rises Tokyo Skytree, one of the world's tallest towers, with observation decks, shopping, and an aquarium at its base. It's an easy add-on to an Asakusa visit and offers sweeping views, especially near sunset.

Why stay here

Asakusa is a popular base for first-timers who want traditional atmosphere and often better value than the western hubs. The trade-off is that it sits on the eastern side, so reaching Shibuya/Shinjuku takes a bit longer — but it's still an easy train ride, and waking up near Senso-ji has its own magic.

Practical tips

  • Visit Senso-ji early or in the evening (the lit-up temple at night is beautiful and uncrowded).
  • Combine Asakusa and Skytree into one easy half-day.
  • The area is walkable and well connected by subway.
  • Carry cash for the small traditional shops.

Bottom line

For old-Tokyo atmosphere — temples, traditional shops, and a slower pace — Asakusa is unmatched in the city. Pair it with the modern spectacle of Skytree next door, and you've got one of Tokyo's most rewarding and characterful areas.

title: Gion & Higashiyama Area Guide (Kyoto)
excerpt: Gion and Higashiyama are Kyoto's most atmospheric districts — preserved streets, major temples, and the geisha quarter. Here's what to see.
content:
The eastern districts of Gion and Higashiyama are the postcard Kyoto — preserved wooden streets, major temples, and the historic geisha quarter, all walkable together. This is where most first-timers fall in love with the city. Here's how to explore it.

Higashiyama's old streets

The Higashiyama district preserves the atmosphere of old Kyoto better than anywhere. The sloping stone lanes of Ninenzaka and Sannenzaka are lined with traditional wooden shops, teahouses, and craft stores, leading up toward Kiyomizu-dera. Wandering these streets — ideally early, before the crowds — is one of Kyoto's great pleasures.

Kiyomizu-dera

At the top sits Kiyomizu-dera, a magnificent wooden temple built on a hillside, with a famous viewing veranda offering sweeping views over Kyoto. It's spectacular in cherry blossom and autumn seasons, and the approach through the old streets makes the visit doubly rewarding. A first-trip essential.

Gion, the geisha district

Gion is Kyoto's historic geisha quarter, full of traditional wooden machiya houses, exclusive teahouses, and lantern-lit lanes — especially atmospheric in the evening. The famous Hanamikoji street is its heart. If you're lucky you may glimpse a geiko or maiko on her way to an appointment.

Gion etiquette

Be respectful: do not chase, block, or grab at geiko/maiko, and follow any posted rules about photography on private streets. They are working professionals, not attractions. Quiet, courteous observation is the way.

More to see nearby

  • Yasaka Shrine: a colorful shrine linking Gion and Higashiyama, lovely when lit at night.
  • Maruyama Park: a popular green space, famous for cherry blossoms.
  • Kodai-ji and other temples: dotted throughout the hills for quieter visits.

How to do it

A great plan: start early at Kiyomizu-dera, walk down through Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka, continue through the Higashiyama temples and Yasaka Shrine, and end in Gion as evening falls for dinner and atmosphere. It's a walkable, full day capturing Kyoto's most beautiful side.

Why stay here

Staying in Gion/Higashiyama puts you amid the charm and within walking distance of major temples, though it can be pricier and busier with day-trippers. For travelers who came to Kyoto for old-Japan beauty, there's no better base.

title: Arashiyama Area Guide (Kyoto)
excerpt: Kyoto's Arashiyama district offers a famous bamboo grove, riverside scenery, temples, and a monkey park. Here's how to visit.
content:
Arashiyama, on Kyoto's western edge, is a district of natural beauty — a famous bamboo grove, a scenic river, temples, and a hillside monkey park. It has a relaxed, resort-like feel, especially once the day crowds thin in the evening. Here's what to see.

The Bamboo Grove

The signature sight is the Arashiyama Bamboo Grove, a path winding through towering bamboo stalks that filter the sunlight into something ethereal. It's short but striking and famously photogenic. Go early in the morning to experience it before the crowds arrive — midday can be very busy.

Tenryu-ji

Beside the bamboo grove sits Tenryu-ji, one of Kyoto's most important Zen temples and a UNESCO World Heritage site, with a celebrated landscape garden that beautifully frames the surrounding hills. Its garden is among the finest in Kyoto and pairs naturally with the bamboo walk.

The river and bridge

The Togetsukyo Bridge spans the scenic Katsura River and is Arashiyama's central landmark, with mountain backdrops that are gorgeous in cherry blossom and autumn seasons. You can stroll the riverbanks or take a traditional boat. The whole riverside area is lovely for a relaxed wander.

The Monkey Park

A hike up the hillside leads to the Iwatayama Monkey Park, where wild Japanese macaques roam freely and you can enjoy panoramic views over Kyoto. It's a steeper walk but fun, especially for families and animal lovers. Follow the posted rules about interacting with the monkeys.

More to explore

  • Okochi Sanso Villa: a beautiful garden estate with views, near the bamboo grove.
  • Temples and shrines: several dot the area for quieter visits.
  • Sagano Scenic Railway: a charming sightseeing train through the valley (seasonal).

How to visit

Arashiyama is on the western edge, so it takes a bit longer to reach from central Kyoto — trains connect it conveniently. Plan a half-day to full day, ideally starting early for the bamboo grove. Pair it with Kinkaku-ji (also on the western/northern side) for an efficient day. For those seeking tranquility and natural beauty, staying overnight in Arashiyama is a peaceful alternative to the central districts.
